title: Courage
hook: courage is not having no fear, but acting while afraid (Joshua 1:9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the race: a cloud of witnesses, every weight laid aside, eyes on Jesus. Your line was run with patience. Did you take one more step in your long race? Day one thousand four hundred ten.

Moses is dead. The man who stood up to Pharaoh, who led the people through the sea, who spoke with God on the mountain, is gone. And the job of leading the whole people across the Jordan falls on his assistant, Joshua. Right there, at the start of the book that carries his name, God speaks to Joshua. And what he says, more than once, isn't a battle plan. It's a sentence meant for someone who is frightened. Nobody tells a calm person not to be afraid. Today: courage.

Here it is, Joshua chapter one, in the King James words: "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." Three things to notice. First, the command comes more than once in that chapter: be strong and of a good courage, again and again, the way you'd steady a friend at the edge of a high dive. Second, God doesn't tell Joshua the danger isn't real. The river still has to be crossed. The land still has to be entered. Third, look at the reason. It isn't that Joshua is strong enough. It's the LORD thy God is with thee. The courage comes from company. So in this text, courage isn't the absence of fear. It's moving forward while afraid, because you aren't alone. Moses had said nearly the same words to Joshua before he died: be strong and of a good courage, he will not fail thee, neither forsake thee. Now there's Esther. She's queen of Persia, and her people are about to be destroyed. Her cousin Mordecai asks her to go to the king uninvited, which could cost her life. He says, "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" And she answers with words that don't sound brave at all: "and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." That's what courage sounds like in Esther's story. Not a cheer. A frightened person deciding to go anyway, and asking her people to fast with her first.
screen: `BE STRONG AND OF A GOOD COURAGE.`
`THE LORD THY GOD IS WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a prayer, and act. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been avoiding because you're afraid. A hard conversation. A doctor's appointment. An apology. A truth you need to tell. Name the fear plainly; there's no need to pretend it away. If you pray, you can pray Joshua's verse, be strong and of a good courage, for the LORD thy God is with thee. If you don't, just breathe with the fear for a minute and notice you're still here. Then pick the smallest first step, and plan to take it today. The bell holds the time.
Courage. In Joshua and Esther, not the absence of fear, but going forward while afraid, because, the text says, God goes with them.
Your line: brave enough. Today, you don't have to be fearless. Just be brave enough for the one first step you chose, and take it. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Christians pray Joshua 1:9 and other verses of courage before surgery, exams, deployments and hard decisions, and churches tell the stories of Joshua, Esther and the saints and martyrs as examples of faith that acted while afraid.

fork.setup: you're Esther. going to the king without being called could cost your life, and your people are in danger. what do you do?
options: stay silent and keep yourself safe.
ask your people to fast, then go in to the king.
send someone else in your place.
fork.reveal: she asks her people to fast with her, then says, so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.

original.note: Hebrew: be strong and of a good courage — God's words to Joshua.

trapdoor: what you thought: courage means not being afraid.
what it means: God tells Joshua be not afraid because God is with him; courage here is acting while afraid.
what a scholar hears: the words be strong and of a good courage come to Joshua from Moses in Deuteronomy, and again from God in Joshua 1, a charge handed from leader to leader.
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it

notes: Joshua as Moses's assistant: Joshua 1:1 calls him 'Moses' minister'; confirm 'assistant'.

Moses's charge to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7–8, 23) is paraphrased in the teach ('be strong and of a good courage, he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee') without quotation marks; confirm wording or keep as paraphrase.
Original: חֲזַק וֶאֱמָץ (Joshua 1:6, 7, 9); confirm pointing and pronunciation.
Esther: queen of Persia; the king is Ahasuerus (KJV). No name given in the script.

Editor pass: God's first words in Joshua 1:2 are about crossing the Jordan, so the hook no longer says 'the first thing he says'; cut 'the river is still high' (Joshua 3:15, not chapter 1); Moses's charge paraphrase now follows Deuteronomy 31:8 ('neither forsake thee'); the word segment attributes God's presence to the text, not the narrator.
Audit: 'what courage sounds like in the Bible' narrowed to Esther's story; garbled 'It isn't you're strong enough' fixed.
